findings.acceptance_test: Either S21 is removed from the source_ids of C11, C55, C82 and C100 (S11 remains as the source, and S21 may stay in the sources list and research_tasks as unopened), or S21 is opened and the three quotations ("creating a character...", "I never had to reject Shawn Carter to become Jay-Z", "a mindless assault"/"behind bars for years") are confirmed against the book text with a page locator. No claim cites an unopened source.

findings.passage: So you go into survival mode, and when you go into survival mode what happen? You shut down all emotions. So even with women, you gonna shut down emotionally, so you can't connect. And then all the things happen from there: infidelity...
findings.problem: Joined quotation. Time prints this as two quotes separated by "he explained", and the primary T Magazine transcript (S4, opened by the verifier via a Wayback raw copy) has an interviewer question and "Yes. In my case, like it's, it's deep." between "can't connect" and "And then all the things...". The article presents it as one continuous quotation without marking the omission. Meaning is preserved, but the quote is not presented as spoken.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage marks the omission (e.g. "...so you can't connect. [...] And then all the things happen from there: infidelity...") or splits it into two quotations, ideally re-quoted from S4. C8 is updated to cite S4 as opened.

The evidence note and C100 are now stale for S4, and S4 is still recorded as access "unavailable".
findings.acceptance_test: S4 is recorded as opened with its locator. The 2017 quotations are attributed to the T Magazine interview (Time may remain as a secondary link). The evidence-note sentence names only Decoded as unopened, or is revised consistently with C100 and its trigger.

findings.problem: In S1 the "when I get big" line comes from a later answer (to Oprah's "And did you know you were angry?", which begins "Yeah. I also felt protective of my mom."), not from the same answer as the "Anger"/"superhero" passage.
findings.acceptance_test: The transition reflects the sequence, e.g. "A moment later in the same conversation he described a job:" or "Asked whether he knew he was angry, he said yes, and that he felt protective of his mother:". The quotation itself is unchanged.

findings.passage: His father answered, "Man, you knew where I was."
findings.problem: In S1 Jay-Z recalls that his father "was saying stuff like 'Man, you knew where I was.'" The words are his approximate recollection, not a verbatim line. "His father answered" presents them as the father's exact words.
findings.acceptance_test: The attribution signals recollection (e.g. "His father, as Jay-Z recalls it, said something like, 'Man, you knew where I was.'"), keeping the protected exchange intact.

findings.problem: Several direct quotations are not inventoried as their own claims, although each was verified against an opened source: Oprah's question "the kind of angry kid who would end up shooting his brother" (S1), "I told him how I felt the day he left" and "He finally accepted that." (S1), "And he passed away." (S1), "So even by your own metrics that doesn't work." (S8), "Are you asking me?" (S7), and the factual line "At 12 he shot his older brother, Eric, in the shoulder" (S1/S12). The standard asks for every direct quote in the inventory.
findings.acceptance_test: Each listed quotation or fact is covered by a claim (new IDs, or by widening the passage of an adjacent claim such as C28, C34, C36, C17 or C66) with source IDs and class.

findings.passage: The second test is what he does when someone else would set the terms, and an honest count matters here because his stated reasons are mixed.
findings.problem: At 4,040 words the body is well above the 2,000-3,500 target. "What separates them" stacks four paragraphs of hedges ("consistent with Eight rather than proof", "weaker on costs than it first looks", "should be held loosely", "No single choice settles it") that partly repeat one another and the strains section. The honesty is right, but the repetition slows the article's most important section.
findings.acceptance_test: The type-comparison sections are tightened by roughly 300-500 words without removing any sourced discriminator evidence (the three tests, the Six/authority observation, the NFL counterexample) or any protected passage. Each limitation is stated once.

findings.problem: The FAQ "Why did Jay-Z turn down the Super Bowl halftime show?" anchors to "What separates them". The refusal and its reasons are told in the untitled opening, and the 2026 acceptance in "Where the Type 8 reading strains", so a reader following the anchor lands on a comparative argument rather than the answer.
findings.acceptance_test: The halftime FAQ anchors to the section that actually narrates the refusal and the 2026 acceptance (e.g. where-the-type-8-reading-strains), or the opening gains a heading whose anchor the FAQ uses.
